title: House Ethics Witness Says She Had Sex With Matt Gaetz at 17
description_medium: During the House Ethics Committee’s investigation, a woman testified that she had sex with Matt Gaetz when she was 17, according to her lawyer and reporting on the closed-door interview. The testimony occurred over multiple days in summer 2024. It became public after Trump selected Gaetz as his attorney general nominee. Gaetz denied the allegations.
description_long: A woman at the center of a House Ethics Committee investigation testified in summer 2024 that she had sex with Representative Matt Gaetz when she was 17, according to reporting based on people familiar with the inquiry and statements by her attorney. The committee subpoenaed her and heard testimony over multiple days. The allegation drew wider attention in November, after Donald Trump nominated Gaetz to be attorney general. Gaetz denied having sex with a 17-year-old and called the allegations false. The witness’s account was testimony in a congressional investigation, not a criminal verdict. In December 2024, the House Ethics Committee released a separate report describing substantial evidence concerning Gaetz’s sexual conduct and payments, including the 2017 encounter; the report did not establish a federal sex-trafficking violation. Distinguishing the original testimony from the later committee report matters because they are separate steps in an inquiry. The direct Trump connection is his nomination of Gaetz, not involvement in the witness’s testimony.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Woman testifies she slept with Matt Gaetz as a minor
corrected_wording.corrected_title: House Ethics Witness Says She Had Sex With Matt Gaetz at 17
corrected_wording.reason: The testimony was about Gaetz; reporting links its public significance to Trump’s attorney-general nomination, not to Trump’s role in the testimony.

source_access_notes: ABC News reported the woman’s summer testimony and her lawyer’s account; the House Ethics Committee report is available through GovInfo.
rationale: Attributes the testimony to the witness and her lawyer, separates it from the later Ethics Committee findings, and identifies Trump’s nomination as the connection to the timeline.

title: Trump Signs Executive Order Expanding Federal Support for State and Local Police
description_medium: On April 28, 2025, Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288, directing federal agencies to expand support for state and local police. It calls for training, equipment, legal resources for officers, and review of consent decrees with local departments. The order also directs Defense and Justice officials to increase access to excess military and national-security assets.
description_long: Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288, “Strengthening and Unleashing America’s Law Enforcement,” on April 28, 2025. The order directs the attorney general to create a mechanism for legal resources and indemnification for officers who incur expenses or liabilities while performing official duties. It tells federal agencies to use federal resources to expand police training, increase officers’ pay and benefits, strengthen legal protections, and improve crime data. It also orders a review of federal consent decrees and agreements with state and local police agencies, with changes or termination when officials determine they unduly impede law enforcement. Separately, the attorney general and defense secretary were directed to increase provision of excess military and national-security assets to local jurisdictions and determine how such assets, training, nonlethal capabilities, and personnel could be used. These are directives for federal agencies to carry out; the order itself does not document a deployment of military personnel or equipment to a particular police department. Its provisions drew debate over federal oversight and police accountability.

corrected_wording.original_title: Police Militarization Executive Order and Law Enforcement Weaponization
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Signs Executive Order Expanding Federal Support for State and Local Police
corrected_wording.reason: The order directs expanded federal support and asset use; the supplied evidence does not establish the broader claims of military occupation or criminalized accountability.

source_access_notes: The executive order text was reviewed directly for the provisions described.
rationale: Replaces unsupported rhetoric with the order’s actual directions, distinguishing planned federal assistance and asset review from a documented deployment.

title: Trump Promotes Hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19; FDA Revokes Stockpile EUA
description_medium: In March 2020, Donald Trump promoted hydroxychloroquine as a possible COVID-19 treatment, calling it a “game changer” and asking, “What do you have to lose?” On June 15, the FDA revoked emergency authorization for stockpiled chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine for certain hospitalized patients, citing little likelihood of benefit and serious cardiac risks. The evidence does not establish that Trump’s remarks caused deaths or shortages.
description_long: Donald Trump publicly promoted hydroxychloroquine as a possible treatment for COVID-19 in spring 2020, describing it as a “game changer” and asking what patients had to lose. At the time, the FDA had authorized use of donated chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine from the Strategic National Stockpile for certain hospitalized patients when clinical-trial participation was unavailable or infeasible. On June 15, 2020, the agency revoked that emergency authorization after reviewing new evidence. The FDA said the drugs were unlikely to be effective for the authorized uses and that potential benefits no longer outweighed known and potential risks, including serious cardiac events. A large randomized trial in hospitalized patients had found no benefit on mortality or speed of recovery. Hydroxychloroquine remains approved for malaria and certain autoimmune conditions, but the COVID-19 emergency authorization was limited to the specified hospitalized-patient setting. The available evidence documents Trump’s promotion and the FDA’s later regulatory decision; it does not demonstrate that his remarks caused particular deaths or medication shortages.

corrected_wording.original_title: Hydroxychloroquine Death Push - Deadly Drug Promotion
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Promotes Hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19; FDA Revokes Stockpile EUA
corrected_wording.reason: The evidence supports Trump’s promotion and the FDA’s risk-based revocation, but not a causal death toll or demonstrated medication shortage.

source_access_notes: FDA’s June 15, 2020 notice supplies the authorization scope and reasons for revocation; the statements attributed to Trump are documented in the supplied timeline context.
rationale: Separates Trump’s public promotion from FDA’s evidence-based revocation and removes unsupported causal claims about deaths and shortages.

title: Trump Names Steven Cheung Communications Director and Karoline Leavitt Press Secretary
description_medium: On November 15, 2024, president-elect Donald Trump named Steven Cheung, his campaign communications director, to lead the incoming White House communications office and selected campaign spokesperson Karoline Leavitt as press secretary. Both appointments carried campaign aides into senior public-facing administration roles and signaled continuity in Trump’s communications team.
description_long: President-elect Donald Trump announced on November 15, 2024, that Steven Cheung would serve as White House communications director and Karoline Leavitt as press secretary. Cheung had led communications for Trump’s 2024 campaign and served as director of strategic response during Trump’s first term. Leavitt had been the campaign’s press secretary and was selected to become the administration’s principal public spokesperson. The two jobs are distinct: the communications director coordinates the president’s broader messaging operation, while the press secretary answers questions and represents the White House in briefings. The selections placed campaign aides in central roles in the incoming administration’s relationship with the news media. Trump also announced Sergio Gor as director of the Presidential Personnel Office in the same transition announcement. These were appointments announced before inauguration, not actions by officials already exercising the duties of those offices. The phrase “bomb thrower” is an opinionated description and is not needed to identify Cheung or his appointment.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump names bomb thrower Steven Cheung as communications director
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Names Steven Cheung Communications Director and Karoline Leavitt Press Secretary
corrected_wording.reason: “Bomb thrower” is editorial characterization; the documented event is the announcement of two White House communications appointments.

source_access_notes: Reuters reported the transition announcement and the White House later listed the appointments in its official staffing announcement.
rationale: Names the two appointments accurately, explains their distinct communications roles, and removes a loaded personal label.

title: Fox News Reports Trump Told Trudeau Canada Could Become the 51st State
description_medium: Fox News reported that Donald Trump suggested Canada could become a U.S. state during a November 29, 2024 meeting with Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at Mar-a-Lago. The report attributed the remark to anonymous sources and placed it in a discussion of tariffs, border security, and trade. The reported joke was not a formal proposal or change in Canada’s status.
description_long: Fox News reported that Donald Trump raised the idea of Canada becoming the 51st U.S. state during a November 29, 2024 meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at Mar-a-Lago. The report attributed the exchange to anonymous people familiar with the meeting; neither a transcript nor an on-the-record confirmation was provided. According to the report, the discussion followed Trump’s threat to impose tariffs on Canadian goods and included border security and trade. Trump reportedly joked that Trudeau could instead become a state governor. The reported remarks were not accompanied by a formal proposal, an agreement between the governments, or a change in Canada’s status. The comment became part of public debate about Trump’s tariff threats and his rhetoric toward Canada. Because the exchange is attributed to anonymous sources, the wording should remain reported speech rather than a confirmed quotation or an official U.S. position.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump tells Trudeau ‘Canada could be America's 51st state'
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Fox News Reports Trump Told Trudeau Canada Could Become the 51st State
corrected_wording.reason: The account attributes the remark to anonymous sources and provides no transcript or on-the-record confirmation.

source_access_notes: The supplied timeline attributes the meeting details to Fox News sources; no transcript or on-the-record account is identified.
rationale: Preserves the reported exchange with explicit anonymous-source attribution and distinguishes it from a formal annexation proposal.

title: Washington Post Reports Loyalty Questions for Trump National-Security Candidates
description_medium: The Washington Post reported in February 2025 that some candidates for senior intelligence and law-enforcement jobs were asked whether the 2020 election was stolen and whether January 6 was an “inside job.” Two candidates who did not answer as desired were not selected, though the report said other factors could have contributed. The White House defended alignment with Trump’s agenda.
description_long: The Washington Post reported that some candidates for senior national-security and law-enforcement positions in the new Trump administration were asked about the 2020 election and the January 6 attack. Two former officials considered for intelligence-community positions said interviewers asked them to answer yes or no to whether January 6 was an “inside job” and whether the 2020 election was “stolen.” They did not give the desired answers and were not selected, although the report said it was unclear whether other factors affected those decisions. At least two candidates for senior FBI field-office jobs were reportedly asked related questions about who won the election, who were the “real patriots” on January 6, and who their “real boss” was; their outcomes were not known. The White House said it was appropriate for national-security candidates to align with Trump’s agenda. The reporting concerns several reported interviews, not a published rule applying to every applicant or a direct presidential interview. It raised concerns about political neutrality in intelligence and law enforcement hiring.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Washington Post Reports Loyalty Questions for Trump National-Security Candidates
corrected_wording.reason: The reporting describes questions posed to some applicants, not a formal universal screening rule or proof that Trump personally asked them.

source_access_notes: The Washington Post article named in the supplied synopsis was located and reviewed; its accounts rely on interviewees familiar with the screening.
rationale: Uses the original Washington Post report, specifies the questions and limits, and avoids generalizing a reported set of interviews into a universal rule.

title: Trump Announces DAMAC Chairman Hussain Sajwani’s Planned $20 Billion U.S. Data-Center Investment
description_medium: On January 7, 2025, president-elect Donald Trump and Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani announced a planned $20 billion investment in U.S. data centers over the coming years. The first phase was described as spanning eight states, including Arizona, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, and Texas. The announcement was a pledge, not completed construction or expenditure.
description_long: At a January 7, 2025, news conference at Mar-a-Lago, president-elect Donald Trump and Hussain Sajwani, chairman of Dubai-based DAMAC Properties, announced a planned $20 billion investment in U.S. data centers over the coming years. Sajwani said the first phase would include projects in Arizona, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, and Texas, and indicated he might invest more later. Trump framed the announcement as support for U.S. technology and artificial-intelligence capacity. Data centers house computing and storage systems used by cloud services and AI applications, making construction capacity a significant infrastructure issue for technology companies. The public announcement did not provide a project-by-project schedule, financing plan, named construction sites, or details of how much money would be spent in each state. It therefore documents an announced corporate intention and its proposed scale, not completed investment or operational facilities. Any assessment of delivery depends on subsequent company and project records.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Hussain Sajwani pledges $20 billion to U.S. data centers
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Announces DAMAC Chairman Hussain Sajwani’s Planned $20 Billion U.S. Data-Center Investment
corrected_wording.reason: “Planned investment” distinguishes the public pledge from completed spending or construction.

source_access_notes: Reuters’ contemporaneous account reports the pledge, its stated time horizon, and the first-phase states.
rationale: Reports the announcement and stated geography while clearly separating a future investment pledge from completed projects.

title: Trump and Melania Trump Launch Meme Coins as Token Values Rise
description_medium: Donald Trump launched the $TRUMP token on January 17, 2025, and Melania Trump announced the separate $MELANIA token two days later. Both tokens rose sharply in reported market value after launch. Market capitalization is an estimate based on token price and supply; it does not establish how much the Trumps or affiliated entities sold or earned. The record does not establish fraud.
description_long: Donald Trump launched the $TRUMP cryptocurrency token on January 17, 2025, two days before his second inauguration. Melania Trump announced a separate token, $MELANIA, on January 19. Both were meme coins, digital tokens whose value can be driven largely by online attention and trading rather than an underlying business or claim on assets. Their prices rose rapidly after launch, producing large reported market-capitalization figures. Market capitalization multiplies a token’s quoted price by its circulating supply; it is not the same as cash received by the issuer or the value that could be realized by selling a large holding. The launches and early price increases alone do not establish the couple’s token allocations, sale proceeds, or investor losses, and a sharp price rise is not proof of fraud. The event is the launch of two branded digital assets and their volatile early trading, which raised questions about conflicts of interest and disclosure as Trump prepared to take office.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump & Melania make billions on ‘meme coin' scam
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump and Melania Trump Launch Meme Coins as Token Values Rise
corrected_wording.reason: The evidence documents two launches and market-price changes but not billions in realized proceeds or fraud.

source_access_notes: The timeline records the launch dates; Reuters’ market report supplies independently reported price and capitalization context.
rationale: Separates token market capitalization from realized proceeds and describes the launches without unsupported claims of fraud or billionaire profits.

title: White House Removes Spanish-Language Website and X Account After Trump’s Inauguration
description_medium: Within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration, the White House removed its Spanish-language website and the @LaCasaBlanca account on X. The administration said the Spanish section was still being developed and would return. The change followed a similar removal in 2017; the website was restored during Joe Biden’s presidency.
description_long: Within hours of Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20, 2025, the White House’s Spanish-language website and its @LaCasaBlanca profile on X were taken offline. The site had provided White House information in Spanish, while the account was the administration’s Spanish-language social-media presence. The removal drew criticism from Hispanic advocacy groups and communications specialists, who said Spanish-speaking residents rely on accessible government information. The administration said the Spanish section was still being developed and would return, framing the change as temporary. The White House had also removed its Spanish-language site after Trump took office in 2017; it was restored under President Joe Biden in 2021. The January 2025 action therefore repeated an earlier transition-era change, but the available announcement did not specify when the site or account would return. The documented change involved one website section and one identified X profile, rather than a list of multiple accounts.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: White House deletes Spanish website and social media accounts
corrected_wording.corrected_title: White House Removes Spanish-Language Website and X Account After Trump’s Inauguration
corrected_wording.reason: AP identifies the Spanish-language site and a specific X profile; the title’s plural “accounts” is broader than the documented change.

source_access_notes: The Associated Press article identifies the website and @LaCasaBlanca profile and reports the administration’s stated explanation.
rationale: Names the specific Spanish-language site and X profile, reports the administration’s explanation, and corrects the unsupported plural framing.

title: Trump Invokes Alien Enemies Act to Deport Venezuelan Men to El Salvador
description_medium: In March 2025, President Donald Trump invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to remove Venezuelan men whom his administration alleged belonged to the Tren de Aragua gang. On March 15, U.S. officials sent 238 Venezuelans and 23 Salvadorans to a prison in El Salvador; 137 Venezuelans were removed under the act, while others were processed under different immigration authorities. The operation prompted emergency legal challenges.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798, asserting that the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua was conducting an invasion of the United States. The next day, U.S. officials sent 238 Venezuelans accused of belonging to the gang and 23 Salvadorans accused of affiliation with MS-13 to El Salvador, where they were held in the country’s terrorism-confinement prison. The Washington Post reported that 137 Venezuelans were removed under the Alien Enemies Act; the remaining Venezuelans and Salvadorans were sent under other immigration authorities. The allegations against individuals were not criminal convictions, and reporting said tattoos were among the indicators used to identify suspected gang members. Some of the Venezuelans had pending immigration hearings. The operation bypassed ordinary immigration proceedings for those removed under the 1798 law and was carried out under an agreement with Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele. It prompted emergency court challenges over presidential authority and whether people could contest their designation before removal.

corrected_wording.original_title: Indefinite Detention Orders, Family Camps, and Alien Enemies Act Revival
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Invokes Alien Enemies Act to Deport Venezuelan Men to El Salvador
corrected_wording.reason: The evidence supports the March deportation operation but does not establish family camps or indefinite detention as described in the original title.

source_access_notes: American Immigration Council and Washington Post reporting identify the transfer totals and legal authorities; the Supreme Court case docket records the emergency litigation.
rationale: Narrows the entry to the March removals, separates Act removals from transfers under other authorities, and distinguishes allegations from convictions.
